title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service recorded private work conversations by default and shared them with the company to train its AI systems without alerting all meeting participants. The service was deployed in professional settings where users did not uniformly consent to data collection, and participants in meetings may not have known their words were being recorded and sent to the company. Catching this would have required the system to obtain explicit informed consent from every participant in a meeting before recording, not just the person initiating the transcript.

The failure occurred at the boundary between a tool designed for note-taking and a data collection system. Even where privacy policies disclosed the practice, the default recording behavior meant conversations could be captured and shared without universal awareness or agreement. Whether users who accepted the terms knew what they were accepting, and whether the company's actual practices matched its disclosures, are questions the lawsuit seeks to establish rather than matters already proven.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording and using private work conversations without permission. The company's Otter Notebook tool, which transcribes virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, records conversations by default and shares them with Otter to improve its artificial intelligence systems without alerting all meeting participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter was secretly recording confidential conversations. The suit alleges the company's practices violate state and federal privacy laws.

The lawsuit highlights privacy concerns that have grown as Otter's use expands, with approximately 25 million users relying on the service to record and process over 1 billion meetings since 2016. Users have reported troubling incidents, including an investor meeting transcription that revealed confidential business details discussed after someone left, and concerns that sensitive conversations with human rights activists could be accessed by foreign governments. While Otter's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training purposes, the suit contends many users remain unaware their conversations are being shared and recorded.
